title: Acute coronary syndromes. NICE guideline NG185
authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
journal: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, published 18 November 2020
result: Recommendations on beta-blockers after myocardial infarction: offer a beta-blocker as soon as possible after a myocardial infarction, when the person is haemodynamically stable (1.4.27, marked 2013); communicate plans for titrating beta-blockers up to the maximum tolerated or target dose (1.4.28, 2013); consider continuing a beta-blocker for 12 months after a myocardial infarction for people without reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (1.4.29, 2020); discuss the potential benefits and risks of stopping or continuing beyond 12 months in such people, including the lack of evidence on the relative benefits and harms of continuing beyond 12 months and the person's experience of adverse effects (1.4.30, 2020); continue a beta-blocker indefinitely in people with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (1.4.31, 2013); do not offer a beta-blocker to people without reduced left ventricular ejection fraction or heart failure whose myocardial infarction was more than 12 months ago, unless there is an additional clinical indication (1.4.33, 2013). Where beta-blockers are contraindicated or need to be discontinued, diltiazem or verapamil may be considered for secondary prevention in people without pulmonary congestion or reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (1.4.35, 2007). Offer all people who have had a myocardial infarction treatment with an ACE inhibitor, dual antiplatelet therapy, a beta-blocker and a statin (1.4.1, 2007, amended 2020).
